name_note — removed on audit: Refuted — one hard factual error plus a structural mis-description of RHS, both in the field prose and in the citations backing it.

Sub-claim by sub-claim against the live pages:

WRONG (drop / correct): "a separate, longer 'Other common names' list of eleven synonyms". The RHS list has THIRTEEN entries, not eleven — the record's own citation quote reproduces all thirteen and contradicts its own count: "American mandrake, behen, devil's apple, duck's foot, ground lemon, hog apple, Indian apple, Indian May apple, peca, raccoon berry, wild jalap, wild lemon tree, wild mandrake". Fix the number to thirteen.

WRONG (structural): "RHS's dedicated species page shows a single 'Common Name' heading of 'May apple' (the page's on-page heading reads 'RHS Plant Profile May apple')", supported by the citation quote "RHS Plant Profile May apple". RHS carries no field or heading labeled "Common Name" anywhere on the page — that label belongs to Missouri Botanical Garden ("Common Name: may-apple"), and attributing it to RHS mis-describes RHS's structure. The quoted string is also synthesized: "RHS", "Plant Profile" and "May apple" are three separate rendered elements stitched into one string presented as verbatim. Real page text to substitute: the document title is "Podophyllum peltatum | May apple" and the profile heading is "May apple".

OVERSTATED: "does not itself include May apple/Mayapple". True only of the bare forms — the list does contain "Indian May apple". Reword to "does not repeat the bare form May apple/Mayapple, though it carries 'Indian May apple'".

ACCURATE AND CITED: MoBot "has a singular Common Name field reading 'may-apple'" (page renders "Common Name: may-apple"), though the note should disclose that MoBot's common-names popup actually lists two entries, "• may-apple • mayapple", so "singular" describes the displayed field, not the page's full common-name data.

ACCURATE AND CITED: NC State "carries only one alphabetized 'Common Name(s)' list (no separate single-name field), whose first entry is 'American Mandrake', with 'Mayapple'/'May Apple' appearing further down that same list" — verified verbatim.

COUNT CHECK: "two of the three admissible sources with dedicated single-species pages (RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden) lead with May apple/may-apple" — the 2-of-3 count is correct. But the sentence then concludes "common_name is set to Mayapple", and neither of those two leads with that closed-compound spelling; the note should say the catalog normalizes the two leading forms to the closed compound rather than implying a source leads with it.

Suggested corrected wording: "Admissible sources split on which common name leads. RHS's dedicated species page is titled 'Podophyllum peltatum | May apple' and its plant-profile heading reads 'May apple', with a separate, longer 'Other common names' list of thirteen synonyms that does not repeat the bare form May apple/Mayapple (it does carry 'Indian May apple'). Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated Plant Finder page has a Common Name field reading 'may-apple' (its common-names popup lists 'may-apple' and 'mayapple'). NC State's Plant Toolbox page, by contrast, carries only one alphabetized 'Common Name(s)' list with no separate single-name field, whose first entry is 'American Mandrake', with 'Mayapple'/'May Apple' appearing further down that same list. Because two of the three admissible sources with dedicated single-species pages lead with May apple/may-apple, common_name takes that name, normalized to the closed compound 'Mayapple' (the form NC State's Description prose and MoBot's common-names popup both use), rather than NC State's alphabetically-first list entry."

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Refuted on completeness and quote fidelity, not on substance — the prose is broadly accurate and unusually thorough, but a safety field cannot ship with a truncated block presented as verbatim plus two missing co-listed traits.

What is correct and verified verbatim: Poison Severity "High" under the human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans:" heading (the record correctly states that scope); the full symptom sentence "The unripe fruit, roots, stems, seeds, and leaves cause salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, excitement, headache, fever, lethargy, panting, and coma (rare)."; the contact sentence "Contact with leaves or roots causes severe redness, irritation, and skin ulcers, especially to the eyes."; Poison Toxic Principle "Podophyllin"; Causes Contact Dermatitis "Yes"; the FULL Poison Part list Leaves/Roots/Seeds/Stems (not truncated); the gloves warning "Protective gloves should be worn while handling any part of this plant because of the potential for severe contact dermatitis."; "All parts of this plant are highly poisonous except for its ripened fruit. The Mayapple contains the toxin known as podophyllotoxin, and it is harmful if ingested."; RHS's "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and its dog-scoped pets line; MoBot's narrower "Leaves and roots are poisonous, however." The field carries the source's own words for the hazard, states the severity rating's human scope, keeps the horse tag out of the pet-toxicity support, and discloses both the parts-list disagreement and the edibility position of two sources. Reproducing both "Podophyllin" (structured field) and "podophyllotoxin" (Description prose) is right.

DEFECT 1 — truncated Edibility block. Both the field prose and the citation labeled "toxicity_detail: NC State's edibility instructions..." end the SAFE HANDLING PROCEDURE at "These products can leave a residue." The live page's block continues one more sentence. Real page text, to substitute at repair: "SAFE HANDLING PROCEDURE: Wash fruit thoroughly with warm water. Do not use dish detergent or any type of sanitizer. These products can leave a residue. The fruit has a lemon-like flavor and can be used to make jams, jellies, and marmalade." A block quoted as verbatim must not stop early.

DEFECT 2 — missing co-listed plant-type traits. NC State's Whole Plant Traits / Plant Type reads "Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Wildflower" — the same species is typed BOTH Poisonous and Edible, which is exactly the tension this field exists to convey, and neither trait is mentioned.

DEFECT 3 — missing the page's own severity banner. NC State prints, immediately under the name, "This plant has high severity poison characteristics." That is the source's own top-of-page hazard statement and belongs in a safety field that already cites the severity rating.

DEFECT 4 — stitched RHS quote. The citation quote "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten" joins two separately rendered blocks into one quoted string, and clips the second mid-sentence. The page renders "Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." (double space) as one block and, separately, "Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". Split into two citations rather than one.

The third citation's label says the field "reproduces NC State's Edibility entry for the young leaves, including its exact preparation time and handling conditions" -- but neither the quote nor the field prose reproduces the entry. Both stop at "...serve like greens." and silently drop the trailing clause. SAFE HANDLING PROCEDURES: Wash leaves in warm water to remove dirt and debris. Do not use dish detergent or any type of sanitizer. These products can leave a residue. Cutting it is a softening in the dangerous direction for a safety field, so it must go back in. records.name_note: RHS's dedicated page leads with 'eastern bluestar'. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a five-item alphabetical list led by 'Blue Dogbane', but its description opens 'Eastern bluestar is a native herbaceous perennial...' and its prose uses that name throughout. Missouri Botanical Garden displays 'blue star' as Common Name (first of a six-item structured list) while its Noteworthy Characteristics prose says 'commonly called eastern bluestar'.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling', then on a separate line 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten' -- the pets line, naming both dogs and cats, is what supports toxic_to_pets=true. NC State says the foliage contains 'a toxic white latex' that makes it resistant to deer and other herbivores; Missouri Botanical Garden says stems and leaves 'produce a milky latex when cut or torn which protects the plant from herbivory' (MOBOT does not call the latex toxic, and handles deer under Tolerate and Problems). Neither NC State nor MOBOT carries a poison block.
unknowns: Common name is contested among admissible sources (see name_note): RHS leads with 'eastern bluestar', NC State's alphabetical Common Name(s) list is led by 'Blue Dogbane' though its prose uses 'eastern bluestar', and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Common Name field gives 'blue star' despite its own prose also saying 'eastern bluestar'.

So MoBot's structured common-name data DOES carry 'eastern bluestar'; it is simply not the display value. The note as written implies MoBot's structured data excludes the chosen name, which is false and materially overstates the disagreement.

Render it the way this record renders its other list quotes (newline-joined), i.e. "Common Name(s):\nBlue Dogbane\nBlue Star\nBlue Star Flower\nEastern Bluestar\nWoodland Bluestar".

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two defects in a safety field; the underlying facts are true, so this is a rewrite, not a value change.

DEFECT 1 — blended hazard wording attributed to sources that do not use it. The field says "NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden each describe the foliage/stems as producing a toxic, milky white latex when cut or torn that deters deer and other general herbivores". No single source says that. The real sentences are:
  NC State: "Drought tolerant once established and resistant to damage by deer and other herbivores due to the foliage containing a toxic white latex." (says toxic, white, foliage, deer — does NOT say 'milky' and does NOT say 'when cut or torn')
  MoBot: "Stems and leaves produce a milky latex when cut or torn which protects the plant from herbivory." (says milky, when cut or torn, stems and leaves — does NOT say 'toxic', does NOT say 'white', does NOT mention deer)
MoBot handles deer in two other places entirely: the Tolerate field ("Tolerate: Deer, Drought, Clay Soil") and Problems ("Deer tend to avoid this plant."). Attributing 'toxic' to MoBot is exactly the kind of hazard word a safety field must take from the source rather than synthesize.

DEFECT 2 — scope collapse on RHS's own warning. RHS's Potentially harmful value is two lines separated by a newline: line 1 "Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" (RHS's unlabelled general/human hazard plus a skin-contact handling warning), line 2 "Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". The record collapses the newline to a space, producing "...protective equipment when handling Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten...", which reads as though the gloves warning applies to handling pets and hides that RHS is flagging a human ingestion hazard AND a handling hazard in addition to the pet hazard. The field also appends a period after "contact numbers" that the page does not have.

ACCURATE AND VERIFIED (keep): RHS's Potentially harmful block genuinely is the only structured toxicity data on that page — there is no poison-part list, no symptom list, and no severity rating. NC State genuinely carries no Poison / Poison Part / Poison Severity / Problem-for-Cats-or-Dogs block for this species (its attribute tree runs Cultural Conditions, Fruit, Flowers, Leaves, Stem, Landscape with no poison section, and its tag list contains no poison tag).

CORRECTED WORDING: "RHS's Potentially harmful section — the only structured toxicity data any admissible source carries for this species — gives two separate lines: 'Harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. The first line is unscoped (RHS's general warning, covering people) and adds a skin-contact handling precaution; the second is the dog- and cat-specific ingestion warning. RHS gives no poison-part list, no symptom list and no severity rating, and NC State carries no Poison or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs block for this species at all. Separately, and in each source's own words: NC State says the plant is 'resistant to damage by deer and other herbivores due to the foliage containing a toxic white latex', and Missouri Botanical Garden says 'Stems and leaves produce a milky latex when cut or torn which protects the plant from herbivory' (MoBot does not call the latex toxic; it lists deer separately under Tolerate and notes 'Deer tend to avoid this plant'). Both are general-herbivore chemical-defence notes, distinct in scope from RHS's human and dog/cat ingestion warning."
